github.title: openai/codex
github.abstract: Codex CLI is a coding agent from OpenAI that runs locally on your computer. If you want Codex in your code editor (VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf), install in your IDE. If you want the desktop app experience, run codex app or visit the Codex App page . If you are looking for the cloud-based agent from OpenAI, Codex Web , go to chatgpt.com/codex . Quickstart Installing and running Codex CLI Run the following on Mac or Linux to install Codex CLI: curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh Run the following on Windows to install Codex CLI: powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c " irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1 | iex " The standalone installers download from https://releases.openai.com/codex by default and fall back to GitHub Releases if a metadata or asset download is unavailable. To force GitHub Releases, set CODEX_INSTALLER_USE_RELEASES_OPENAI_COM to false ( 0 and no are also accepted): curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | CODEX_INSTALLER_USE_RELEASES_OPENAI_COM=false sh $ env: CODEX_INSTALLER_USE_RELEASES_OPENAI_COM = ' false ' ; irm https: // chatgpt.com / codex / install.ps1 | iex Codex CLI can also be installed via the following package managers: # Install using npm npm install -g @openai/codex # Install using Homebrew brew install --cask codex Then simply run codex to get started. You can also go to the latest GitHub Release and download the appropriate binary for your platform. Each GitHub Release contains many executables, but in practice, you likely want one of these: macOS Apple Silicon/arm64: codex-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz x86_64 (older Mac hardware): codex-x86_64-apple-darwin.tar.gz Linux x86_64: codex-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz arm64: codex-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz Each archive contains a single entry with the platform baked into the name (e.g., codex-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl ), so you likely want to rename it to codex after extracting it. Using Codex with your ChatGPT plan Run codex and select Sign in with ChatGPT . We recommend signing into your ChatGPT account to use Codex as part of your Plus, Pro, Business, Edu, or Enterprise plan. Learn more about what's included in your ChatGPT plan . You can also use Codex with an API key, but this requires additional setup . Start a free 14-day trial → Type /graphify in your AI coding assistant and it maps your entire project (code, docs, PDFs, images, videos) into a knowledge graph you can query instead of grepping through files. Each connection is tagged EXTRACTED (explicit in the source) or INFERRED (resolved by graphify), so you can tell what was read directly from what was inferred. Not a vector index. No embeddings, no vector store: a real graph you traverse. Ask a question, trace the path between two things, or explain one concept. Note Want this always-on? Get started (30 seconds). Needs Python 3.10+ and uv (or pipx): uv tool install graphifyy # install the CLI (or: pipx install graphifyy) graphify install # detects your assistant and registers the skill Then, in your AI assistant: /graphify . github.abstract: FreeLLMAPI 7.4 billion tokens per month.  34 free LLM providers. 635 free model endpoints. One OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Aggregate free tiers from dozens of providers, plus custom OpenAI-compatible chat, embedding, image, and audio endpoints, behind a single /v1 API. Keys are stored encrypted. A router picks the best available model for each request, falls over to the next provider when one is rate-limited, and tracks per-key usage so you stay under every free-tier cap. freellmapi.co · browse the full catalog: 474 model families, 635 free endpoints English · 簡體中文 · Русский · O'zbekcha Your router updates its own model catalog from a signed feed: new free models, quota changes, and compatibility fixes land without a git pull . Free installs get the monthly snapshot, so a model reaches them 30 days after it joins the live feed; premium routers get it the same day. Go live at freellmapi.co ($19/yr, cancel anytime). On its own each tier is a toy. Stacked together, they add up to roughly 7.4 billion tokens per month of working inference capacity, across 474 model families / 635 provider endpoints from small-and-fast to reasonably capable. The problem is that stacking them by hand is painful: thirty-four different SDKs, thirty-four different rate limits, thirty-four places a request can fail. FreeLLMAPI collapses that into one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Point any OpenAI client library at your local server, and it routes transparently across whichever providers you've added keys for. And the free-tier landscape shifts weekly: providers launch models, retire them, and change quotas without notice. FreeLLMAPI tracks all of that for you. The router pulls a signed model catalog from freellmapi.co on its own, so your install keeps up without a git pull . See Premium (live catalog) for how fast it keeps up. Monty the Clapper — the official mascot of OpenMontage OpenMontage The first open-source, agentic video production system. Paste A Video · Quick Start · Try These Prompts · Pipelines · How It Works · Providers · Review Guide · Agent Guide Follow The Build Turn your AI coding assistant into a full video production studio. Describe what you want in plain language — your agent handles research, scripting, asset generation, editing, and final composition. Important distinction: OpenMontage can make image-based videos, but it can also make a real video video for free/open-source workflows: the agent builds a corpus from free stock footage and open archives, retrieves actual motion clips, edits them into a timeline, and renders a finished piece. That is not the usual "animate a handful of stills and call it video" trick. signal-from-tomorrow_final_with_music_upload_v2.mp4 "SIGNAL FROM TOMORROW" — a cinematic sci-fi trailer fully produced through OpenMontage: concept, script, scene plan, Veo-generated motion clips, soundtrack, and Remotion composition. the_last_banana_v3_github.mp4 "THE LAST BANANA" — a 60-second Pixar-style animated short about a lonely banana who finds friendship with a kiwi. 6 Kling v3-generated motion clips (via fal.ai), Google Chirp3-HD narration, royalty-free piano music, TikTok-style word-level captions, and Remotion composition. Total cost: $1.33 . objects-in-overdrive-github.mp4 "OBJECTS IN OVERDRIVE" — a 54-second, music-driven 3D showcase featuring ten objects with distinct choreography: gravity-shifting furniture, frozen car drifts, cloth impacts, refractive lenses, moving gears, an acrobatic robot, and more. Custom Blender animation and physics, kinetic typography, and a phonk soundtrack. Rendered with Blender Eevee/Cycles and assembled with FFmpeg. No narration. reimagine-your-universe-github.mp4 "Reimagine Your Universe" — a 50-second vertical transformation film in which one visual idea moves across objects, eras, materials, and scale. Five generated motion scenes, sparse Google Chirp narration, a Pixabay score, and a bespoke HyperFrames composition turn separate clips into one authored cinematic journey. Total cost: about $4 . products-come-to-life-github.mp4 "Products Come to Life" — a 60-second product film built from approved hero stills. Five hard-surface products separate into their own engineering and reassemble, with each still pinned as the first and last frame so the model invents motion without losing product identity. Image-to-video generation, bespoke sound, narration, and a custom composition complete the film. openmontage-model-showcase-github.mp4 "Imagine the Possibilities with OpenMontage" — seven generated worlds collected into one music-only showcase. Three image models supply campaign, fashion, and miniature-world artwork; four video models expand the journey through architecture, material transformation, a living greenhouse, and a creature encounter. OpenMontage animates the stills, edits the motion, unifies the soundtrack, and closes with Monty the Clapper. Source generation cost: about $5 . final-github-under-10mb.mp4 "How Salt Made History" — a 100-second cinematic documentary about the mineral that funded empires, shaped trade routes, sparked revolutions, and gave us the word “salary.” Real-world footage is woven together with original narration and hand-authored motion graphics for its etched title, etymology reveal, animated maps, historical timeline, and closing thesis. final-github-under-10mb.mp4 "One Prompt Built This Complete 3D World" — a continuous 60-second journey through one coherent, editable fantasy world. Distinct terrain regions, an inhabited village, waterways, ruins, dense vegetation, and a late hero-landmark reveal are assembled from textured 3D assets, then brought together with cinematic lighting, atmospheric music, and a planned camera path. Subscribe to @OpenMontage on YouTube to see new videos as they ship — every video includes the full prompt, pipeline, tools used, and cost so you can reproduce it yourself. Start From A Video You Already Love Starting from a reference video is often faster than starting from a blank prompt. OpenMontage can start from a YouTube video, Short, Reel, TikTok, or local clip and turn it into a grounded production plan: Paste a reference video The agent analyzes transcript, pacing, scenes, keyframes, and style You get 2-3 differentiated concepts, an honest tool path, cost estimates, and a sample before full production "Here's a YouTube Short I love. Make me something like this, but about quantum computing." What you get back is not "best guess prompt spaghetti." You get: What it keeps from the reference: pacing, hook style, structure, tone What it changes : topic, visual treatment, angle, narration approach What it will cost at your target duration, before asset generation starts What it will actually look like with your currently available tools Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf, Codex — any AI coding assistant that can read files and run code. Watch It Happen — The Backlot Living Storyboard Chat tells you what the agent said . Backlot shows you what the production is actually doing — a local board that fills itself in as the pipeline runs. Stages light up, the script lands as a screenplay page, scene cards shimmer while assets generate, and every provider decision and dollar spent is on the wall. When a production starts, the agent opens it for you automatically. No setup, no reporting — the board derives everything from the project files the pipeline already writes. The storyboard is now a real approval gate. Asset generation pauses on a scene-by-scene contact sheet — takes, prompts, per-asset cost, quality scores — so you approve the visuals before the render, not after it's too late: Creative gates hold until you answer. The board shows what's waiting and why; you reply in chat: Every production on your machine, live-first, in the library: python -m backlot open # the library — every project on disk python -m backlot open < project-id > # one production's live board python scripts/backlot_simulate_run.py # no production yet? watch a simulated one live And when a run is done, hit ▶ REPLAY RUN — the whole production replays from its timestamps, scrubbable end to end. See backlot/README.md for how it works. Use real footage only, no narration, elegiac tone, with music." That's it. The agent researches your topic with live web search, generates AI images, writes and narrates the script with voice direction, finds royalty-free background music automatically, burns in word-level subtitles, and renders the final video. Before you see anything, the system runs a multi-point self-review — ffprobe validation, frame sampling, audio level analysis, delivery promise verification, and subtitle checks. Every provider selection is scored across 7 dimensions with an auditable decision log. Every creative decision gets your approval. Open-source orchestration for teams of AI agents. If OpenClaw is an employee , Paperclip is the company . Paperclip is a Node.js server and React UI that orchestrates a team of AI agents to run a business. Bring your own agents, assign goals, and track work and costs from one dashboard. Choose models and harnesses per agent while keeping your team's tasks, skills, permissions, and history in one place. It looks like a task manager. Under the hood: org charts, budgets, governance, goal alignment, and agent coordination. Manage business goals, not pull requests. Step Example 01 Define the goal "Build the #1 AI note-taking app to $1M MRR." 02 Hire the team CEO, CTO, engineers, designers, marketers — any bot, any provider. 03 Approve and run Review strategy. Set budgets. Hit go. Monitor from the dashboard. Nasiko is the OpenRuntime for agents, coding harnesses, frameworks and tools. Find the coding agents already running. See what each one costs, by harness and model. Route them to the models you choose while developers keep using their existing harness workflows. 📚 Documentation • 💬 Discord • 🐛 Report a bug Table of Contents What is Nasiko? Start here: see what is already running Coding agents: reporting and routing Features Why this runs in the call path Architecture Requirements Quick Start: Docker only (no Rust needed) Setup guides by operating system Deploying your own agents Environment Variables Project Structure Troubleshooting Project Activity Documentation & Links Support Contributing License What is Nasiko? Your developers are already running coding agents. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, often
more than one at a time, each with its own dashboard and its own billing unit. At the end of the
month there is a real bill, and nobody can say who spent it, on which model, or what it produced. Nasiko finds those agents, puts their spend in one schema, and hands back the model choice the
harness made for you. An OpenRuntime belongs to no vendor inside it: your cost history, your policy
and your model choice stay with you rather than with whichever harness you happened to install. Two properties hold the rest of this together, and they are not the same thing. Non-invasive discovery is about your architecture. Nasiko can detect the harnesses you already
run without changing their configuration. Reporting and routing are explicit opt-ins that add hooks
or update harness settings, but they require no wrapper or SDK in your application code. Non-intrusive operation is about your day. After one-time setup, developers keep using the same
harness commands and interfaces. OpenCode must be restarted after its plugin is installed, and
Codex asks you to trust the new Nasiko hooks. Nasiko Dashboard : deploy agents, route traffic, manage tools, and watch traces. Start here: see what is already running Install the current CLI from this checkout, then run its read-only discovery command: git clone https://github.com/Nasiko-Labs/nasiko.git && cd nasiko
cargo install --path cli/ --force
nasiko agents discover nasiko agents discover reads your machine, prints what it finds, and exits. You get a row per
supported harness: whether it is detected, whether it is reporting to Nasiko, its version, and
where its config lives. Discovery changes no harness settings, requires no account, and sends
nothing off the machine. If nasiko agents discover is not listed by nasiko agents --help , reinstall with the --force command above. Older builds use the same 0.1.0 version number, so nasiko --version alone cannot tell you whether the command is present. Harness Discovery and session reporting LLM routing Claude Code yes yes Codex yes yes OpenCode yes yes Cursor CLI yes not yet Those four are the supported set today and we will continue to add support for me. If you have a request please create an issue! The CLI is a Rust crate, so this path needs Rust . Reporting and routing also
need an active control plane and valid login: see Quick Start . Coding agents: reporting and routing Nasiko manages the coding-agent CLIs already installed on your machine: it can record what they
do, route their LLM calls, or both. The two are independent opt-ins. agents uninstall removes
local reporting hooks but preserves the registered agent and its history; disconnect restores
routing settings, though a running harness may need to be stopped or disconnected with --force . Session reporting nasiko agents discover # DETECTED / CONNECTED / VERSION / CONFIG per agent nasiko agents install < agent > # claude, codex, opencode, or cursor nasiko agents install < agent > --no-content # omit prompt and response text nasiko agents uninstall < agent > nasiko agents sync # flush queued session-turn events to the control plane Auto-install also fires on nasiko connect <control-plane-url> , nasiko use , and nasiko auth login , but only when authenticated and only for agents with no existing install
record . Routing commands such as nasiko connect claude do not trigger auto-install. Nasiko never
silently rebinds an already-installed agent to a new cluster; rebind explicitly with nasiko agents install <agent> . Nasiko installs each harness's supported event hooks: Claude uses Stop , OpenCode reports on session.idle , and Codex and Cursor use their richer hook event sets. Completed turns are queued
locally under ~/.nasiko/integrations/queue/ and delivered to POST /api/telemetry/coding-agent/events/batch , so a control plane that is briefly unreachable
costs you nothing. Permanently-failed deliveries (after a cluster is deleted or renamed, say) land
in ~/.nasiko/integrations/rejected/ and are safe to delete. Ingested turns show up as chat sessions right away ( nasiko sessions , nasiko history <id> ).
Traces, token counts, and cost additionally require CODING_AGENT_OTLP_ENDPOINT , covered below. Routing: give the harness back the model choice Some harnesses arrive tied to a provider by default. Claude Code defaults to Anthropic; Codex
defaults to OpenAI. That choice arrived with the tool rather than with you. Register a provider and key with Nasiko once, then point a harness at Nasiko instead of at its
vendor. Inbound wire protocol and outbound provider are decoupled, so an Anthropic-format request
from Claude Code is served by your OpenAI key: nasiko llm-config create --name my-openai --provider openai --model gpt-4o \
  --api-key-secret OPENAI_API_KEY --secret-value " $OPENAI_API_KEY " nasiko connect claude --config my-openai The full set of bindings: nasiko connect claude --config < llm-config-name > nasiko connect codex --config < llm-config-name > nasiko connect opencode --config < llm-config-name > nasiko disconnect < agent > # reverse the settings/plugin changes nasiko status < agent > # show current binding connect claude configures Claude Code's apiKeyHelper and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL . connect codex adds a model_providers.nasiko entry and command-based auth to Codex's config.toml . Their
credential helpers obtain a one-hour JWT from POST /api/agents/{id}/llm-token ; Codex refreshes
its credential on a timer rather than minting one for every request. Claude Code sends the
credential in the x-api-key header rather than Authorization ; the router accepts both. connect opencode instead installs plugins/nasiko-llm-router.js under OpenCode's config
directory (respecting OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR and XDG_CONFIG_HOME ), registers a nasiko provider,
and makes nasiko/router the default model for new OpenCode sessions only. OpenCode fixes a
session's model at creation time in its own database, so resuming an existing session will not
route it. Start a new one, or pick "Nasiko Router" explicitly. Inbound wire protocol and outbound provider are fully decoupled: nasiko connect claude --config my-openai-config routes Claude Code's Anthropic-format traffic to OpenAI. ~/.claude/settings.json and OpenCode's config are per-user, global files. Connecting an agent
affects every Claude Code / OpenCode process on the machine, not just the current project. LLM config management nasiko llm-config create --name < name > --provider < provider > --model < model > nasiko llm-config list
nasiko llm-config update < name > [--provider ...] [--model ...]
nasiko llm-config set-default < name > nasiko llm-config attach < name > --agent < agent > # attach to a deployed agent nasiko llm-config detach --agent < agent > nasiko llm-config get < agent > # resolved routing config for an agent nasiko llm-config providers # valid provider/model values + pricing Set a config's model for predictable routing. If it is unset, the router falls back through tier
models and then the platform default; list shows provider/? for the unset value. Server configuration Everything is env-driven. server/.env.

Hex Speak. It appears. Local-first voice dictation, built in Rust. Download for Mac, Windows, or Linux · Windows beta · Linux beta · TypeScript SDK · Contributing Hex is local-first voice dictation for Apple silicon Macs running macOS 15 or
newer. Hold a shortcut, speak, and release. Hex transcribes on your Mac and
pastes the result into the app you are using. On-device transcription. Download a local speech model during setup;
ordinary dictation does not require OpenCode or a cloud transcription service. Your words, your way. Choose a shortcut, language, and model. Use Modes for
corrections, application-specific behavior, and optional text processing. The macOS app is available now. The Windows beta covers x64 and
ARM64 PCs, and the Linux beta covers x86_64 X11 and compatible
wlroots Wayland compositors. See Privacy and local data for what stays on your device and what optional features send to a provider. Install Hex Downloads Stable is the current release. Dev is the newest build of dev , published
on every change; it updates itself from the Dev channel. Platform Stable Dev macOS (Apple silicon) DMG DMG Windows x64 Installer Installer Windows ARM64 Installer Installer Linux x86_64 Executable Executable Linux x86_64 (Debian, Ubuntu) .deb .deb Linux x86_64 (Fedora, openSUSE) .rpm .rpm Linux ARM64 Executable Executable Linux ARM64 (Debian, Ubuntu) .deb .deb Linux ARM64 (Fedora, openSUSE) .rpm .rpm macOS updater ZIP ZIP Windows x64 updater EXE EXE Windows ARM64 updater EXE EXE On Arch Linux you can also use yay -S hex-bin , or the install script below. With Homebrew: brew install --cask anomalyco/tap/hex Then launch Hex from Applications and complete setup. The cask installs the same signed app and keeps its built-in updater. Existing
DMG installations can keep using Check for Updates ; Homebrew does not migrate
or forcibly replace another app already named Hex.app . Or install manually: Download the signed DMG and open it. Drag Hex.app into Applications, then launch it. Complete the permission and model steps in setup. Microphone lets Hex record while you dictate. Accessibility lets Hex notice its shortcut in every app and paste into the foreground app. Drag the Hex tile into the list. Hex does not need Input Monitoring. Transcription model downloads the speech model that runs locally. Hex checks for signed updates automatically. Use Hex > Check for Updates… to check immediately. Organizations that manage app versions themselves can turn off in-app updates,
including manual checks, with the DisableUpdates Boolean in the anomaly.hex preference domain. Deploy it in a configuration profile
(payload type anomaly.hex , key DisableUpdates , value true ), or for a
single Mac run defaults write anomaly.hex DisableUpdates -bool true . On
Windows, set the DWORD DisableUpdates to 1 under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Anomaly\Hex (Group Policy) or the same path in HKCU.
Relaunch Hex to apply it. Model downloads still work. Releases through 2.3.1
used the com.kitlangton.hex2 domain; profiles for those keep applying only to them. Download blocked? Each app release on GitHub Releases has the identical signed files. App releases use v… tags ( app-v… through
2.3.1); the repository also publishes separate TypeScript SDK releases.
If an older installation cannot check for updates on your network, install the
DMG manually over the existing Rust app. On managed networks, ask IT to allow anoma.ly : Hex downloads and updates
from the Anomaly release service at https://anoma.ly/release (releases up to
2.3.1 use https://anoma.ly/hex/files ). Local model setup separately needs huggingface.co and its model
download CDN. A successful
app download does not establish that those model hosts are reachable. After
restoring access, retry model preparation in Settings. Coming from the original Swift app? Install the new app manually and complete
setup. Settings and history are not transferred. Quit the old app before
dictating in the new one so their shortcuts do not compete. Dictate Anywhere Hold Option , speak, then release. Hex transcribes and pastes at the current
focus. Double-tap Option to keep recording; press Option again to finish. Press Escape to cancel. While recording, Escape discards the recording; after
you release, it cancels the newest dictation that is still transcribing, so
nothing is pasted for it. Press Option-Shift-V to paste the last completed dictation again. Settings let you change the shortcut, microphone, language, local model,
recording behavior, feedback volume, launch-at-login behavior, and Dock
visibility. Corrections in Modes fix names and preferred spellings before text
is pasted; modes can also apply optional rewriting and text transformations. Use menu bar > Transcription Model to switch between downloaded models without
opening Settings. Each model remembers its last selected language and, for
Whisper, recognition hints. Choose the language in Settings once, then switch
between combinations such as English with Parakeet and French with Whisper from
the menu. Manage Models… opens the full picker for downloads and language changes. Optional OpenCode Features OpenCode is optional, and ordinary dictation does not
require it. Hex never launches OpenCode: these features use an OpenCode service
that is already running, and say "OpenCode isn't running" otherwise. Post-processing: enable OpenCode in Modes to rewrite a transcript before
paste. Hex sends the transcript, foreground application, and Brave website
hostname to the configured model provider. Modes can target applications and
websites in Brave Browser. If OpenCode rewriting fails, Hex keeps the corrected local transcript and still
runs any selected text transformations. If that transformation stage fails, Hex
keeps the text from before the stage, not partial transformation results. Annotate Annotate records your screen while you draw on it and talk, then hands the
recording to an agent: its keyframes, your drawing, and a transcript of what
you said. It is on by default on macOS and Linux (Settings › Annotate; not on
Windows yet). Nothing is recorded, and no screen permission is asked for,
until you first use it. One key: Option-Shift-S on macOS, F9 on Linux. Tap it to start
and tap again to stop. While it records, hold it and move the pointer to
draw, no click needed; let go and the mouse is the app's again. macOS asks
for Screen Recording the first time; Linux asks through the desktop's
screen-sharing dialog once, then remembers the screen. While it records,
the dictation shortcut does nothing. The bar: the recording bar at the top shows the timer, a pen (click it,
then drag to draw like a real pen; click it again or press Esc to stop), stop, and ✕ to
discard. On macOS, holding Shift draws too. Ink fades from the screen
after about a second but stays in the recording. Paste or send: when it stops, the annotation is on your clipboard and
the capsule offers Paste (the contact sheet, then the summary) and Inspect . With OpenCode running, Send to… lists its sessions (macOS
also opens its suggestions by itself): click one to send it there, and Undo
takes it back for a few seconds. A send carries the transcript and the
pictures inline, so it works with an OpenCode server on another machine. hex annotate list|show|send (also hex capture … ) reads and sends from the
terminal. Custom Transformations Advanced users can create ~/.config/hex/hex.config.ts for deterministic
dictation transformations, written in TypeScript or JavaScript. Hex runs the
config itself in an embedded JavaScript engine and reloads it on save; nothing
else needs installing. hex commands init creates the starter workspace, and hex commands check reports what the config registers or why it fails. Config scripts get no filesystem, network, or process access.

others.title: Secure Multi-Agent Collaboration Using Large Language Models
others.abstract:
As Large Language Models have emerged and become increasingly significant, the way to develop smart multi-agent
systems has been transformed, enabling them to communicate, collaborate and decision more efficiently. These systems rely on
agents working independently which need to effectively and safely coordinate their actions, to maintain reliability in messy realworld environments. However, bringing LLMs into the mix introduces new risks like data leaks, trickery from bad actors, and
trust issues. This paper breaks down a full plan for keeping multi-agent teamwork secure when using LLMs. We look at
everything from how they are built and the rules they use to communicate to the safety tools used to stop attacks. We also talk
about where this is being used now, the hurdles we still face, and where the tech is headed for building secure AI ecosystems

others.title: VAANIX: A Real-Time Voice AI Agent Platform with Action-Enabled Agents, Automated Appointment Booking and a Business Workspace
others.abstract:
Telephone support is still the main way many small businesses talk to their customers, yet it is also the channel they
are least able to staff around the clock. Traditional IVR menus frustrate callers, and most of the newer AI voice products are
closed, priced per minute and difficult to adapt to a specific business. This paper presents VAANIX, a self-hostable voice agent
platform that connects ordinary phone calls to a streaming pipeline of speech recognition, a large language model and speech
synthesis, so that a caller can simply talk and be understood. The first version of the platform focused on that conversational
pipeline and a developer console. In this paper we describe a second, larger iteration. A single Agent Studio now holds
everything about an agent: its prompt, voice, knowledge base, API settings, call logs, single calls and bulk calling. Agents can
also be given actions at creation time. The most important of these is appointment booking, in which the agent checks
availability while the caller is still on the line, books the slot, and confirms it by voice. Confirmed bookings appear immediately
on a Business Workspace home screen that shows a calendar of the client's own appointments instead of generic call statistics.
We explain the architecture, the action mechanism, the way double bookings are prevented, and the security design built on row
level isolation. Manual testing across all modules showed that callers receive a spoken reply typically within one to two seconds
and that booked slots are reflected on the calendar within moments, without the per-minute platform fees charged by managed
voice agent services.

others.title: AI-Based College Transportation Management
others.abstract:
Colleges that run their own buses usually plan transport using fixed routes and estimated student counts. In practice,
the number of students who actually travel changes from day to day, so some buses run with many empty seats while others are
overcrowded. This paper presents the design of the AI-Based College Transportation Decision Support System, a full-stack web
application that collects daily travel confirmations from students and uses rule-based software agents to analyse route-wise
demand, check route compatibility, recommend bus allocation, and suggest seat optimization within capacity limits. Every
recommendation is accompanied by a plain-language explanation, and no change becomes final until the administrator
approves it. The previous allocation stays in force until a replacement plan is approved. The system is built with React.js,
Node.js, Express.js and MongoDB, with JWT-based authentication and role-based access control. It uses predefined rules and
calculations only; it does not use machine learning, GPS tracking, or external generative AI services. This paper describes the
problem, the system architecture, the database design, the rule-based algorithms, and an illustrative worked example.
Experimental evaluation on real college data is identified as future work.

others.title: Black Swan: Stock Crash Predictor
others.abstract:
Global financial markets have grown so interconnected and fast-moving that spotting a high-impact event before it
hurts investors' portfolios has become a serious challenge. This project introduces "Black Swan: Stock Crash Predictor," an AIdriven system built to catch unpredictable global events early and gauge how they are likely to ripple through financial markets,
using a combination of Generative AI and Agentic AI. Rather than waiting for a crisis to unfold, the system keeps a constant
watch over news outlets, RSS feeds, financial reports, and live market feeds, flagging emerging risks such as geopolitical
conflict, pandemics, economic downturns, and supply-chain breakdowns as they surface. Generative AI is used to turn this raw
information into readable summaries, forward-looking narratives, and impact assessments, so investors can make sense of
complicated situations quickly. Agentic AI adds a further layer of autonomy, allowing the system to reason independently, make
decisions on its own, and keep adjusting to shifting market conditions. It also runs automated stress-testing simulations and risk
assessments to gauge how markets and investments might behave under uncertainty. Where conventional monitoring tools tend
to fall behind fast-changing events, this approach is built to keep pace, offering proactive alerts that give investors an early
warning. Overall, the framework is aimed at sharpening key decision-making factors: response time, prediction accuracy, market
awareness, and investment strategy planning.

others.title: A TIERED LIFECYCLE GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK FOR AGENTIC ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN FINANCIAL SERVICES
others.abstract: The rapid emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) presents significant governance challenges for financial services, where autonomous systems increasingly support high-impact financial activities. Existing regulatory approaches remain fragmented and continue to rely primarily on non-binding supervisory guidance, leaving important gaps in lifecycle oversight, accountability, and systemic risk management. This paper proposes the Tiered Lifecycle Governance (TLG) Framework, a strategic governance model that integrates lifecycle-based AI oversight with responsive, risk-based regulation. The framework combines three transaction-risk tiers with four AI lifecycle stages to establish proportionate oversight obligations that balance innovation, regulatory accountability, and financial stability. Drawing on technological, economic, legal, and institutional perspectives, the framework is applied to the 2026 U.S. interagency review of model risk management guidance (SR 26-2) to demonstrate how lifecycle governance can strengthen oversight of agentic AI in financial services. The analysis shows that the TLG Framework provides a structured alternative to the existing guidance-versus-rulemaking approach by aligning regulatory obligations with transaction risk rather than institutional size or technology labels. The paper concludes that binding, lifecycle-based oversight offers a practical pathway for improving resilience, transparency, and accountability in financial AI governance while providing a transferable governance model for other emerging AI policy domains.

others.title: AI-Assisted Web Server Log Interpretation Using LLaMA Model
others.abstract:
Modern web infrastructures generate large volumes of access logs that contain valuable information related to system
activity, user behaviour, performance monitoring, and cybersecurity threats. Manual analysis of these logs is time-consuming,
error-prone, and inefficient for detecting suspicious activities in real time. This project presents the design and implementation
of a Local AI System for Log Interpretation using LLaMA models, capable of performing automated log analysis, anomaly
detection, AI-assisted summarization, and conversational log investigation within a privacy-preserving local execution
environment. The system integrates Django-based operational management, Linux scheduling utilities (Cron and At), quantized
GGUF(GPT-Generated Unified Format) LLaMA models, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) techniques to support
both scheduled analysis workflows and interactive “Chat with AI” operations. The log files uploaded/access from read-only
specified location are passed to the AI inference engine, where log parsing, OWASP-based threat detection, contextual analysis,
and structured JSON response generation are performed using locally deployed LLaMA models.
Through CPU-compatible inference utilising llama-cpp-python, the project maintains lightweight deployment while enabling
instantaneous, recurring, and scheduled analysis execution. GPU-accelerated environments such as Google Colab and Kaggle
were additionally utilized for large-scale inference evaluation and high-volume log processing experiments. The conversational
RAG workflow enables users to interact directly with uploaded logs using natural language queries and receive AI-generated
cybersecurity insights, suspicious activity explanations, and remediation recommendations.
Experimental evaluation demonstrates reliable task execution, efficient response generation, structured report handling, and
effective contextual reasoning capabilities for both scheduled analysis and conversational AI-assisted workflows. The proposed
system provides a modular, privacy-preserving, and locally deployable solution for intelligent cybersecurity log analysis and
operational threat interpretation.

others.title: CONSTRUCTING PROFESSIONAL IDENTITIES IN AI-ENHANCED LANGUAGE CLASSROOM: A STUDY OF PAKISTANI ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHERS’ PERSPECTIVES AND PRACTICES
others.abstract: The main aim of the study is to investigate the construction of English Language Teachers’ (ELTs) professional identity in the Artificial Intelligence (AI) era in the Pakistani Punjab context. The qualitative analysis is embedded in semi-structured interviews. Multilayered sampling techniques were used, and data were collected from ELTs working in public and private educational institutions and analyzed using the Grounded Theory Approach (GTA). Initially, purposive sampling was used to identify appropriate samples, and those samples referred additional samples until saturation was attained on the thirteenth sample. The investigation was theoretically informed by Gee’s (2000) distinction between I-identity and A-identity. Findings created five interrelated categories: Institutionally Framed Professionalism, Agentive Professional Self, Constrained Autonomy, Negotiation Professional Identity, and Hybrid Identity Construction. Results highlight that examination-driven systems, curricular mandates, and administrative checks and balances powerfully form ELTs’ identities. They are sustained simultaneously by contemplative practice, adaptive strategies, and professional achievement. Autonomy was developed as conditional rather than absolute, leading teachers to negotiate between organizational compliance and personal pedagogical obligation. The study demonstrates that ELT identity in Punjab is dynamic, context-sensitive, and permanently negotiated. By integrating hierarchical and agentive dimensions of identity, this research contributes to a nuanced understanding of teacher professionalism within examination- focused educational systems.

others.title: LAYER 2 OF THE AI-FIRST SDLC: A PROPOSED AGENT-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURE FOR BUILD, VALIDATION, AND RELEASE READINESS
others.abstract: This paper proposes Layer 2 of the AI-First Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) introduced in our parent framework and extended through the Layer 1 Product and Designer Layer. Layer 2 is a conceptual Build, Validate, and Release architecture intended to transform a Product Requirement Bundle (PRB) and a Design Artifact Bundle (DAB) into a documented, validated, merge-ready pull request. It defines six proposed specialist agents—Architecture, Coding, Testing, Review, PR, and CI Gate—coordinated by a Layer 2 Sub-Orchestrator. The design includes a bounded Feedback-Driven Repair Loop, revalidation after code modifications, non-overridable CI and security gates, and a mandatory human merge decision. The proposed design draws on the authors' technical analysis, review of existing software-engineering and agentic-AI approaches, and exploratory proof-of-concept work. The integrated architecture has not been implemented or empirically evaluated; potential effects on delivery time, code quality, cost, and compliance remain hypotheses for future evaluation.

others.title: AI Fitness OS: Verifiable, Multi-Metric Fitness Guidance by Constraining a Large Language Model with Deterministically Computed Targets
others.abstract:
Fitness applications usually record one behaviour in isolation, and large-language-model (LLM) coaches produce
fluent advice whose numbers are rarely checked. This paper presents AI Fitness OS, a web application that keeps training,
nutrition, hydration, sleep, weight, steps and goals in one per-user record, computes every numerical target deterministically
from published equations and stated heuristics, and passes those targets to Google Gemini as binding constraints; each
generated meal plan is re-checked in code against a ±5 % tolerance. The premise was examined through secondary research on
a public dataset of 2,111 records, and the artefact through tests, simulation and live measurement. All eight lifestyle metrics that
the system tracks or addresses were significantly associated with obesity level (Bonferroni-adjusted α = 0.00625), although only
three remained so on 515 records resembling the original survey. A Random Forest that combined the eight metrics reached a
macro-F1 of 0.720 against 0.263 for the best single metric (Wilcoxon W = 55, p = 0.00098). Across 1,000 simulated user profiles,
every constrained meal plan fell within ±5 % of its calorie target, against 75 of 1,000 unconstrained plans (exact McNemar p <
10⁻²⁰⁰). The calculator agreed with the dataset's weight-category labels for 98.82 % of records, and live responses took 2.5–6.1 s
at no cost. The findings support computing arithmetic, generating language and checking the output against the computed
numbers.

others.title: FROM AIOPS TO AGENTOPS: SERVICE-LEVEL OBJECTIVES AND ERROR-BUDGET-GOVERNED AUTONOMY FOR PRODUCTION AI AGENTS
others.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now run production workflows, including IT and network operations, yet they are usually monitored with signals designed for deterministic services: availability, latency, and error rate. An agent can satisfy all three while completing the wrong task. This paper extends AIOps-style service management to agentic systems. It contributes a layered set of service-level indicators (SLIs) covering platform health, step-level tool use, verified task outcomes, and guardrail integrity; a taxonomy of seven agent failure classes mapped to the signals that expose them; and an error-budget policy that governs an agent's autonomy as well as its release cadence. A Monte Carlo simulation of a production operations agent evaluates the approach across 2,100 injected incidents. Conventional platform monitoring detected only platform failures, firing in at most 1.7% of runs for the other six classes. Burn-rate alerting on verified task outcomes detected every class in 89.7% to 100% of runs within 24 hours, with no false alarms, but took a median of 3.5 to 10.6 hours under standard thresholds. A change-aware rule, active for six hours after a deployment or model change, cut median detection of change-induced regressions to 44 to 63 minutes at a cost of about one additional page per month. The results support layered, outcome-based service-level objectives as the operational basis for production agents.

others.title: EVALUATING PATH EFFICIENCY AND WHEEL DYNAMICS ACROSS VARYING TURNING RADII IN WHEELED MOBILE ROBOTS
others.abstract: Mobile robots navigating within indoor confined spaces generally use various turning techniques to negotiate obstacles and corners. Although zero radius turns (R=0.0 m) allow saving space, the continuous-arc approach provides different possibilities related to such factors as energy, duration, and wheel slip. This paper proposes an analysis of the performances of a mobile robot based on a simulation carried out using the Python programming language and NumPy package. The study examines a model of a differential-drive robot making a 90-degree turn at different radii (R ∈ {0.0,0.2,0.5,1.0,2.0}m). On the basis of the kinematic analysis along with power and slip estimations, it has been demonstrated that small radii (for example, R=0.2 m) reduce greatly the duration of the manoeuvre (0.78 s) and save space, although they increase significantly the power peaks (6.30 W) and slip peaks (0.0141). In its turn, large radii (R=2.0 m) decrease mechanical slips and power peaks but increase energy consumption (37.92 J) and manoeuvre duration (7.85 s). Composite Efficiency Index indicates that larger arcs lead to increased efficiency per joule, while small turns increase speed efficiency. These simulation findings give us a mathematical basis for determining adaptive turns depending on operating conditions, such as choosing between battery life and time efficiency.

others.title: ATLAS - Where Travel Meets AI: An AI-Powered Travel Planning and Decision-Support Platform with Live Data Grounding
others.abstract:
Travel planning is a fragmented, multi-domain decision process: a traveller must separately research destinations,
transport, accommodation, food, activities and weather before assembling a feasible schedule. This paper presents ATLAS
(“Where Travel Meets AI”), an implemented AI-powered travel planning and decision-support platform that pairs a large language model (LLM) planner with deterministic grounding against live geospatial and environmental data. Given a destination,
an inclusive date range, a boarding location, a budget and traveller preferences, ATLAS generates a day-by-day itinerary with
the open-weight gpt-oss-120b model served through Groq, while route, weather, food and accommodation agents run concurrently and record the provenance of each data source. Model output is validated rather than trusted: a schema enforces exactly
one itinerary day per requested calendar date, generated place names are resolved through OpenStreetMap’s Nominatim geocoder, and road distances and travel times are computed with OSRM from the traveller’s real boarding location, with unknown
legs reported as unavailable instead of zero. The system is implemented as a React and TypeScript single-page application
backed by FastAPI and PostgreSQL, and includes a live weather outlook, real restaurant and attraction listings, a simulated
booking flow that issues a PDF e-ticket by e-mail, and a community Lost & Found module. We describe the architecture and
grounding method, report a verification suite of 477 automated tests and preliminary functional observations, and state the system’s current limitations explicitly

others.title: HOW RELIABLE ARE LAYER COMPARISONS FROM SMALL PROBING DATASETS
others.abstract: Probing classifiers are used to compare the linguistic information available at different layers of a language model. These comparisons often rely on limited labelled data, although additional training examples can change which layer performs best. We study the accuracy lost when a layer is selected from a small probing dataset and then evaluated with a probe trained on more data. Experiments across encoder and decoder models show that changes in the selected layer are frequent, but many produce little loss in accuracy. Larger losses depend on the checkpoint and, within the examined Qwen3 family, concentrate in the smaller models. In most such cases, the initially selected layer has higher test accuracy with limited data, but another layer benefits more from additional training. Simple geometric scores often make less accurate choices than a fitted linear probe. Controlled experiments also show how feature scaling affects the regularized probe without removing information. Finally, uncertainty estimates for fixed probes do not consistently predict selection errors after further training. The findings support evaluating the accuracy cost of layer selection directly and distinguishing uncertainty about current predictions from changes caused by additional training data.

others.title: A Study on the Process of Constructing Generative AI Image Prompts Using Hairstyle Search Interest: Focusing on Google Trends Analysis and the Procedural Application of the PDCA Framework
others.abstract: This study aimed to analyze online search interest in hairstyle-related terms and to explore a procedure for converting the results into a data-based structured prompt for generative AI hairstyle image creation. The PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) framework was used as a procedural framework. Google Trends data for seven hairstyle-related terms were analyzed from April 2021 to March 2026, and Sleek Cut, which showed the highest Recent Interest Ratio (2.03), was selected as the case hairstyle. Based on hair design elements and prompt engineering studies, the prompt was structured into Basic, Detailed, and Control elements using R and applied to Google Gemini 20 times to generate 20 images. Three hair and beauty experts independently evaluated the images using five criteria. The overall mean was 4.50, with form showing the highest score (M=4.63) and color the lowest (M=4.15). Average-measure ICCs ranged from .887 to .968, with an overall ICC of .948, indicating high inter-rater agreement. Based on these results, color-related prompt elements were identified as requiring further refinement. The Act stage was limited to deriving improvement directions and did not include regeneration or re-evaluation. These findings suggest that online search-interest data can be used as an exploratory basis for selecting hairstyle visualization targets and systematically structuring prompt elements for generative AI.

others.title: SECURING THE AI-FIRST SDLC: IDENTITY, ACCESS, AND DATA PROTECTION FOR ENTERPRISE AI AGENTS
others.abstract: AI agents can now participate in several steps of software delivery: reading requirements, changing code, requesting tests, and preparing releases. Giving them this freedom creates a difficult security question. How can an enterprise allow useful work without giving an agent more authority than the task requires? Existing practices such as least privilege, identity management, separation of duties, and audit logging provide much of the foundation. The challenge is applying them consistently when a human delegates work to agents that use several connected systems. This paper proposes Agentic Identity and Access Governance (AIAG), a security framework for the AI-First Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC). Four connected mechanisms define the proposal: a Role Conflict Matrix that checks the combined permissions of people and their sponsored agents; an Agent Access Manifest that records permitted tools and operating limits; a governed boundary between live personal-information access and general AI-assisted work; and an MCP Gateway that enforces access policy before tool calls execute. A customer notification-preference change is used to explain how these mechanisms affect development, testing, release approval, and support. We also describe credential handling, data-egress controls, audit, and practical ways to evaluate the framework. The work is conceptual, informed by technical analysis and exploratory proof-of-concept activity. No end-to-end deployment or measured security results are claimed.
